PROP
4
REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Repeals prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns. Public funding programs may not use funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety. Fiscal Impact: Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs. Supporters: League of Women Voters of CA; California Nurses Association; Mental Health Advocacy; Social Security Works; Consumer Watchdog Opponents: California Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; Family Business Assn of California; United Latinos Action
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: State and local governments could create public campaign financing programs for public office candidates, subject to limits on which public funds could be used, how the public funds could be used, and who could receive them.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: State and most local governments would remain unable to create public campaign finance programs for public office candidates.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES ON 4. California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns— communities in all other 49 states have this right. Special interests want to keep the ban to protect their power. Prop. 4 removes it. Strict taxpayer safeguards. Vote YES: Elections should be won, not bought.
CON
Prop. 4 allows politicians to use YOUR taxpayer money to fund their negative campaigns. Prop. 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money they can get. Worse yet, Prop. 4 allows SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY IN POLITICS. NO ON PROP. 4.
FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
FOR

# Proposition 4: Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding
## Proposition 4: Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns. Legislative Statute.
### Additional Titles
Public Fundraising, Allow Public Financing of Election Campaigns Measure
### Summary
Proposition 4 was placed on the ballot by Senate Bill 42 (SB 42).
SB 42 changes provisions of the Political Reform Act of 1974, which bans the use of public funds for candidates’ political campaigns.
The senate passed the bill in June 2025, with the Assembly passing it in September 2025.
Gov.
Gavin Newsom signed the bill in October, sending it to the ballot as Proposition 4.
Proposition 4 would remove California’s prohibition on using public money to finance political candidates, allowing state and local governments to establish publicly funded campaign programs in the future.
The measure would not itself create such a program, but would give governments the option to develop their own systems within statewide guidelines.
Under the measure, funds dedicated to purposes such as education, transportation, and public safety could not be redirected to campaigns.
Candidates receiving public financing would have to demonstrate a sufficient level of support among voters and comply with spending limits and other program requirements.

## Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns
Repeals the ban on public financing of campaigns and allows state or local governments to establish programs that provide candidates with public funding under preestablished spending limits and eligibility requirements.
...
Proposition 4 would give state and local jurisdictions the option of creating a public financing program for candidates running for office.
If state and local governments opt in, they would have to develop spending limits and criteria for candidates to qualify for public funds.
Candidates would be barred from using public finance dollars for legal defense fees, fines, or to repay personal loans to a campaign.
The source of funding, such as a city’s General Fund or a property tax, is left to local governments, but the funds cannot come from money earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety.
...

The legislature addressed this issue in 2025, resulting in Prop.
4 on the 2026 ballot.
...
Current state law permits public campaign financing only in charter cities, not at the state level or in non-charter cities.

4 was placed on the ballot legislatively through Senate Bill 42 (2025) and requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.

### Summary
Proposition 4 was placed on the ballot by Senate Bill 42 (SB 42).
SB 42 changes provisions of the Political Reform Act of 1974, which bans the use of public funds for candidates’ political campaigns.
The senate passed the bill in June 2025, with the Assembly passing it in September 2025.
Gov.
Gavin Newsom signed the bill in October, sending it to the ballot as Proposition 4.
Proposition 4 would remove California’s prohibition on using public money to finance political candidates, allowing state and local governments to establish publicly funded campaign programs in the future.
The measure would not itself create such a program, but would give governments the option to develop their own systems within statewide guidelines.

### Analysis of Measure
#### Proposal
***New Bond for Natural Resources and Climate Activities.*** Proposition 4 allows the state to sell a $10 billion bond for natural resources and climate activities.
Much of the bond money would be used for loans and grants to local governments, Native American tribes, not-for-profit organizations, and businesses.
Some bond money also would be available for state agencies to spend on state-run activities.
***Funding Would Pay for a Variety of Activities.*** As shown in Figure 1, Proposition 4 pays for activities within eight broad categories, each with different goals.
Some of the main activities in each category are summarized below:
- ***Drought, Flood, and Water Supply ($3.8 Billion).*** Roughly half of this money would be for activities to increase the amount and quality of water available for people to use ($1.9 billion).
This would include storing water so it can be used during future droughts, as well as cleaning polluted water to make it safe to drink.
Money would also be used to help reduce the risk of floods, such as by repairing dams and capturing and reusing stormwater ($1.1 billion).
The rest of the money would be used for various activities, such as restoring rivers and lakes.

# Proposition 4
Authorizes Bonds for Safe Drinking Water, Wildfire Prevention, and Protecting Communities and Natural Lands From Climate Risks.
Legislative Statute.
### Analysis of Measure
#### Proposal
***New Bond for Natural Resources and Climate Activities.*** Proposition 4 allows the state to sell a $10 billion bond for natural resources and climate activities.
Much of the bond money would be used for loans and grants to local governments, Native American tribes, not-for-profit organizations, and businesses.
Some bond money also would be available for state agencies to spend on state-run activities.
***Funding Would Pay for a Variety of Activities.*** As shown in Figure 1, Proposition 4 pays for activities within eight broad categories, each with different goals.
Some of the main activities in each category are summarized below:
- ***Drought, Flood, and Water Supply ($3.8 Billion).*** Roughly half of this money would be for activities to increase the amount and quality of water available for people to use ($1.9 billion).
This would include storing water so it can be used during future droughts, as well as cleaning polluted water to make it safe to drink.
Money would also be used to help reduce the risk of floods, such as by repairing dams and capturing and reusing stormwater ($1.1 billion).
The rest of the money would be used for various activities, such as restoring rivers and lakes.

### Analysis of Measure
#### Proposal
***New Bond for Natural Resources and Climate Activities.*** Proposition 4 allows the state to sell a $10 billion bond for natural resources and climate activities.
Much of the bond money would be used for loans and grants to local governments, Native American tribes, not-for-profit organizations, and businesses.
Some bond money also would be available for state agencies to spend on state-run activities.
***Funding Would Pay for a Variety of Activities.*** As shown in Figure 1, Proposition 4 pays for activities within eight broad categories, each with different goals.
Some of the main activities in each category are summarized below:
- ***Drought, Flood, and Water Supply ($3.8 Billion).*** Roughly half of this money would be for activities to increase the amount and quality of water available for people to use ($1.9 billion).
This would include storing water so it can be used during future droughts, as well as cleaning polluted water to make it safe to drink.
Money would also be used to help reduce the risk of floods, such as by repairing dams and capturing and reusing stormwater ($1.1 billion).
The rest of the money would be used for various activities, such as restoring rivers and lakes.

The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects.
Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California, as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure.
But Prop 45 also plunged underwater.
Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.

How this is built
Proposition 4 is forecast as a government and ethics measure whose Yes vote leans Democratic . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. Polls then pull the forecast toward them by recency and size, after splitting undecided voters two to one for No. Sources: elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ccrov/2026/june/26179jj.pdf), growsf.org (https://growsf.org/news/2026-07-02-14-state-measures/), ppic.org (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), escholarship.org (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf). How this is built
Proposition 4 is forecast as a government and ethics measure whose Yes vote leans Democratic . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Repeals prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns. Public funding programs may not use funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety. Fiscal Impact: Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs. Supporters: League of Women Voters of CA; California Nurses Association; Mental Health Advocacy; Social Security Works; Consumer Watchdog Opponents: California Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; Family Business Assn of California; United Latinos Action
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: State and local governments could create public campaign financing programs for public office candidates, subject to limits on which public funds could be used, how the public funds could be used, and who could receive them.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: State and most local governments would remain unable to create public campaign finance programs for public office candidates.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES ON 4. California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns— communities in all other 49 states have this right. Special interests want to keep the ban to protect their power. Prop. 4 removes it. Strict taxpayer safeguards. Vote YES: Elections should be won, not bought.
CON
Prop. 4 allows politicians to use YOUR taxpayer money to fund their negative campaigns. Prop. 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money they can get. Worse yet, Prop. 4 allows SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY IN POLITICS. NO ON PROP. 4.

# Proposition 4: Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding
## Proposition 4: Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns. Legislative Statute.
### Additional Titles
Public Fundraising, Allow Public Financing of Election Campaigns Measure
### Summary
Proposition 4 was placed on the ballot by Senate Bill 42 (SB 42).
SB 42 changes provisions of the Political Reform Act of 1974, which bans the use of public funds for candidates’ political campaigns.
The senate passed the bill in June 2025, with the Assembly passing it in September 2025.
Gov.
Gavin Newsom signed the bill in October, sending it to the ballot as Proposition 4.
Proposition 4 would remove California’s prohibition on using public money to finance political candidates, allowing state and local governments to establish publicly funded campaign programs in the future.
The measure would not itself create such a program, but would give governments the option to develop their own systems within statewide guidelines.
Under the measure, funds dedicated to purposes such as education, transportation, and public safety could not be redirected to campaigns.
Candidates receiving public financing would have to demonstrate a sufficient level of support among voters and comply with spending limits and other program requirements.
